chunks: "I2C needs two signal wires, SDA for data and SCL for clock, and a common ground so everybody agrees what a zero is. Each device only needs those two pins.
Then there's one pull-up resistor on each line, shared by the whole bus, because the drivers are open-drain. If I have more slaves, I don't add wires.
I just tap them onto the same SDA and SCL, and they're told apart by their 7-bit address, so the master sends the address first and only the matching slave answers.
That's the big advantage over SPI, where every extra slave needs another chip-select. The limits are practical.
First, addresses: there are 112 usable, and two identical parts, say two of the same temperature sensor, will collide unless they have address-select pins.
If they do collide I'd use an I2C multiplexer like a TCA9548 amps, which gives me eight separate downstream buses, or put them on a second I2C peripheral.
Second, capacitance: every pin and every centimetre of trace adds to the bus capacitance, and the spec caps it at 400 picofarads.
With too many devices the rising edges get too slow, so I'd lower the pull-up value, slow the clock down, or split the bus with a buffer or switch."
